title: Welcoming seekers
hookLine: Sikhs welcome seekers without pressing anyone to convert

cards: A first-time visitor stands at the gurdwara door, unsure. Shoes? Head?
Is it all right to be here at all? Someone notices. A scarf is offered for covering the head.
A hand points: over there, the langar, if you're hungry. Nobody asks what the visitor believes. Nobody hands over a sign-up sheet.

The visitor eats, listens to the kirtan for a while, maybe asks a question, and leaves when they like. That ease isn't the accident of one friendly person. It runs through the way the Gurus dealt with seekers.

teach.h: GURU ARJAN: A FRIEND TO EVERYONE.
teach.b: First, a friend to all. A hymn of Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to everyone. The posture toward a stranger starts there, not with a sales pitch.

We've sat with the Siddhas twice already; look at the Sidh Gosht once more, this time for its manner. The yogis test Guru Nanak with hard questions. He answers, verse by verse; they push back, and he answers again.
Nobody is shamed for asking. A seeker's question is worth a careful answer. Third, no pressure.
The Gurus' own stories favor invitation over insistence: Guru Nanak traveling, singing, talking with whoever came. Anyone may sit in the sangat, eat in the langar, hear the Granth read.
Some who come later choose to take amrit and join the Khalsa.
That choice is theirs, and it's meant to be free, or it means nothing.
It's easy to welcome someone who agrees with you. It's harder to welcome the person whose question sounds like a challenge, or who leaves unpersuaded.
The Gurus' way treats that person as a guest, fed and honored, not a project.

how: Gurdwaras are open to visitors of any background, who are asked only to cover their heads, remove their shoes and refrain from tobacco and alcohol; the langar serves everyone, and taking amrit is a personal choice.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, and a band of yogis meets you with sharp questions about your path. what do you do?
o: refuse to talk with people who doubt you.
answer each question carefully and let them push back.
insist they join you before you'll explain.
games.why: the Sidh Gosht is that conversation: question and answer, verse by verse, with no one shamed for asking.

practice: Recall a question someone once asked you about something you care about, your faith, your work, your family's ways, that made you bristle. Breathe in and hear it again without the bristle.
Breathe out and imagine answering the way you'd pour tea for a guest: unhurried, warm, with no need for them to agree.

wordCard.voice: Welcoming seekers. Sikhs welcome anyone to the gurdwara and the langar, answer questions as Guru Nanak did in the Sidh Gosht, and leave the choice free. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sidh Gosht, the conversation with the Siddhas, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: welcome, not pressure. A guest is free to leave still deciding. Until tomorrow.
